Exploring `data/processed/models_clean.csv`, the 3,000 most downloaded models on the Hugging Face Hub (collected November 4, 2026) joined with their linked arXiv papers.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BLUE, ORANGE, GRAY = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#52514e"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.titlelocation": "left"})

models = pd.read_csv("data/processed/models_clean.csv", parse_dates=["created_at", "last_modified", "first_paper_date"])
print(models.shape)
models.head()
```

# Overview

```{python}
print("Missing values per column:")
print(models.isna().sum()[models.isna().sum() > 0])
```

```{python}
models[["downloads_30d", "downloads_all_time", "likes", "params_billions", "age_days", "num_arxiv_papers"]].describe().round(1)
```

Downloads and likes are extremely skewed. The median model has about 2.2 million all-time downloads and 58 likes, but the top model (`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`) has 4.2 billion downloads. Everything below uses medians and log scales.

# Who uploads the top models?

```{python}
print("Distinct authors:", models["author"].nunique())
models["author"].value_counts().head(10)
```

OpenMed alone has 315 models in the top 3,000. 237 of them were created on the same day (2025-07-16), which is a bulk upload of medical token-classification models.

```{python}
print(models[models["author"] == "OpenMed"]["task"].value_counts().head(3))
print(models["created_at"].dt.date.value_counts().head(3))
```

# Task

```{python}
by_task = models.groupby("task").agg(n=("model_id", "size"), median_downloads=("downloads_all_time", "median"), median_likes=("likes", "median"))
by_task["median_downloads"] = by_task["median_downloads"] / 1e6
by_task = by_task[by_task["n"] >= 30].sort_values("n", ascending=False)
by_task.round(1)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Median all-time downloads and likes by task, for tasks with at least 30 models."
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal bar charts. Left: fill-mask has the highest median downloads at about 19 million, then sentence-similarity. Right: image-to-image and text-to-image have the highest median likes, token-classification the lowest."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
by_task.sort_values("median_downloads").plot.barh(y="median_downloads", ax=axes[0], color=BLUE, legend=False, width=0.6)
axes[0].set_title("Median all-time downloads (millions)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("")
by_task.sort_values("median_likes").plot.barh(y="median_likes", ax=axes[1], color=ORANGE, legend=False, width=0.6)
axes[1].set_title("Median likes")
axes[1].set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Downloads and likes point in different directions. `fill-mask` models (BERT and friends) have the highest median downloads (18.6 million) but few likes. `image-to-image` and `text-to-image` get the most likes.

# Library and license

```{python}
by_lib = models.groupby("library").agg(n=("model_id", "size"), median_downloads=("downloads_all_time", "median"), median_likes=("likes", "median"))
by_lib[by_lib["n"] >= 20].sort_values("n", ascending=False).round(0)
```

```{python}
lic = models["license"].value_counts()
print("Share apache-2.0:", round(lic["apache-2.0"] / len(models), 3))
print("Share mit:", round(lic["mit"] / len(models), 3))
lic.head(10)
```

```{python}
by_lic = models.groupby("license").agg(n=("model_id", "size"), median_downloads=("downloads_all_time", "median"), median_likes=("likes", "median"))
by_lic[by_lic["n"] >= 20].sort_values("median_likes", ascending=False).round(0)
```

Permissive licenses dominate: 55% apache-2.0 and 14% MIT. The model-specific licenses (gemma, llama) have far more likes per model, but those are big-lab releases, so it is the lab and not the license.

# Size

```{python}
print("Models with a parameter count:", models["num_parameters"].notna().sum())
models.groupby("size_class", observed=True).agg(n=("model_id", "size"), median_downloads=("downloads_all_time", "median"), median_likes=("likes", "median")).round(0)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Parameters vs all-time downloads, both on a log scale. Point size is likes."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of 1,832 models. Downloads do not rise with parameter count. The biggest, most liked points are over 10B parameters but sit in the middle of the download range."
has_size = models[models["num_parameters"] > 0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
ax.scatter(has_size["num_parameters"], has_size["downloads_all_time"], s=5 + has_size["likes"] / 40,
           color=BLUE, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.5)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Parameters")
ax.set_ylabel("All-time downloads")
ax.set_title("Bigger models are liked more, not downloaded more")
for _, row in has_size.nlargest(4, "likes").iterrows():
    ax.annotate(row["model_id"].split("/")[-1], (row["num_parameters"], row["downloads_all_time"]), fontsize=8, color=GRAY, xytext=(5, 5), textcoords="offset points")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Likes by size class (log scale)."
#| fig-alt: "Box plot of likes for four size classes. Median likes climb from about 12 for models under 100M parameters to about 160 for models over 10B."
order = ["under 100M", "100M to 1B", "1B to 10B", "over 10B"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.boxplot([models.loc[models["size_class"] == s, "likes"] + 1 for s in order], tick_labels=order,
           widths=0.5, patch_artist=True, boxprops=dict(facecolor=BLUE, alpha=0.5), medianprops=dict(color="black"))
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_ylabel("Likes + 1")
ax.set_title("Likes climb with parameter count")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
print("Correlation of log parameters with log downloads:", round(has_size["num_parameters"].apply("log10").corr(has_size["downloads_all_time"].apply("log10")), 3))
print("Correlation of log parameters with log likes:", round(has_size["num_parameters"].apply("log10").corr((has_size["likes"] + 1).apply("log10")), 3))
```

Median downloads barely move across size classes (2.3M to 3.8M), and the smallest models are actually downloaded the most. Median likes go from 12 (under 100M) to 162 (over 10B).

# Likes vs downloads

```{python}
print("Correlation of log likes and log downloads:", round((models["likes"] + 1).apply("log10").corr(models["downloads_all_time"].apply("log10")), 3))
print("\nMost liked:")
print(models.nlargest(5, "likes")[["model_id", "likes", "downloads_all_time"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nMost liked per download (loved but not used):")
print(models.nlargest(5, "likes_per_million_downloads")[["model_id", "likes", "downloads_all_time"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nFewest likes per download (used but not loved):")
print(models[models["likes"] > 0].nsmallest(5, "likes_per_million_downloads")[["model_id", "likes", "downloads_all_time"]].to_string(index=False))
```

# Time

```{python}
print("Models with a real creation date:", models["created_at_known"].sum())
models["created_year"].value_counts().sort_index()
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Models created per year among the top 3,000, for the five most common tasks. Models with the placeholder 2022-03-02 date are left out, and 2026 only runs through November 4."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart from 2022 to 2026. text-generation and image-text-to-text grow every year and dominate 2025 and 2026. token-classification spikes in 2025 from the OpenMed upload."
top_tasks = models["task"].value_counts().head(5).index
by_year = models[models["task"].isin(top_tasks)].groupby(["created_year", "task"]).size().unstack("task")[top_tasks]
colors = [BLUE, ORANGE, "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4"]
ax = by_year.plot.bar(figsize=(9, 5), color=colors, width=0.8, edgecolor="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Year created")
ax.set_ylabel("Models")
ax.set_title("Newer top models are mostly text and image-text generation")
ax.set_xticklabels([int(y) for y in by_year.index], rotation=0)
ax.legend(title="", frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
print(models.groupby("created_year")[["downloads_all_time", "downloads_30d", "likes"]].median().round(0))
```

Older models have more all-time downloads (they have had longer), but the 30-day downloads are flat or higher for new models.

# Papers

```{python}
print("Models with at least one arXiv paper:", (models["num_arxiv_papers"] > 0).sum())
print(models["paper_category"].value_counts().head(6))
print("\nDays from first paper to model creation:")
print(models["days_paper_to_model"].describe().round(0))
print("\nShare of models created before their paper:", round((models["days_paper_to_model"] < 0).mean(), 3))
```

```{python}
models.groupby(models["num_arxiv_papers"] > 0)[["downloads_all_time", "likes"]].median().rename(index={True: "has paper", False: "no paper"}).round(0)
```

Half of the models link a paper, and those models get more likes. cs.CL (language) papers outnumber cs.CV (vision) 903 to 329. The median gap from paper to model is 76 days, and a quarter of models were on the Hub before the paper was posted.
